title: Immunology
summary: Innate and adaptive defences, antibodies, vaccines and disorders.

layers.basics: The immune system recognises and removes threats. Innate defences respond fast and generally; adaptive defences respond specifically and remember.
layers.deeper: Barriers, phagocytes and inflammation form the first response. B and T lymphocytes recognise specific antigens, make antibodies and kill infected cells, and memory cells give lasting protection after infection or vaccination.
layers.expert: Immune responses balance defence and tolerance. Failures cause allergy, autoimmunity or immunodeficiency; manipulating them underlies vaccines, transplants and cancer immunotherapy.

title: Innate immunity: barriers, phagocytes and inflammation

layers.basics: Skin, mucus and acid block most invaders. Phagocytes (neutrophils, macrophages) engulf microbes and inflammation brings more cells.
layers.deeper: Complement proteins mark and kill microbes; interferons warn neighbouring cells about viruses; fever helps.
layers.expert: Pattern-recognition receptors (Toll-like receptors) detect PAMPs. NF-κB drives cytokine release; neutrophil extracellular traps catch microbes. Sepsis is a dysregulated systemic response.

layers.basics: Cells display protein fragments on MHC molecules. T cells check these fragments to decide whether a cell is infected or foreign.
layers.deeper: MHC I (on all nucleated cells) presents to CD8⁺ cytotoxic T cells; MHC II (on dendritic cells, macrophages, B cells) presents to CD4⁺ helper T cells.
layers.expert: HLA genes are the most polymorphic in humans (> 30,000 alleles). Matching HLA is key for transplants. The thymus selects T cells that recognise self-MHC but not self-peptides.

layers.basics: Helper T cells coordinate other immune cells; cytotoxic T cells kill infected or cancerous cells.
layers.deeper: Naive T cells activate in lymph nodes after meeting antigen with co-stimulation, then expand ≈ 10,000-fold.
layers.expert: T cell receptors are generated by V(D)J recombination (repertoire ≈ 10¹⁵ theoretically). Regulatory T cells enforce tolerance; checkpoint receptors (PD-1, CTLA-4) restrain responses.

layers.basics: B cells make antibodies that bind antigens, marking them for destruction or neutralising them.
layers.deeper: Antibody classes: IgM (first), IgG (most abundant), IgA (mucosal), IgE (allergy), IgD. Plasma cells secrete thousands of antibodies per second.
layers.expert: Antibodies are Y-shaped with two heavy and two light chains; variable regions give specificity. Somatic hypermutation and class switching refine responses in germinal centres; affinity often rises ≈ 10–1,000-fold.

title: Antibody and receptor diversity (V(D)J)
summary: Generating a vast repertoire from few genes.

layers.basics: Gene segments are cut and pasted in developing lymphocytes to make a unique receptor in each cell.
layers.deeper: RAG1/2 enzymes drive the rearrangement. Junctional diversity and hypermutation add more variation.
layers.expert: The potential repertoire exceeds 10¹¹ antibodies. Tonegawa received the 1987 Nobel for explaining this. Immune repertoire sequencing now tracks clones during disease and vaccination.

layers.basics: When an antigen meets the matching lymphocyte it multiplies. After infection some cells remain as memory cells.
layers.deeper: Primary responses take ≈ 1–2 weeks; secondary responses peak in ≈ 2–3 days with far more antibody.
layers.expert: Burnet's clonal selection theory (1957) is a cornerstone of immunology. Memory B-cell and long-lived plasma cell pools can last decades; some antigens (influenza) drift and evade memory.

layers.basics: A vaccine shows the immune system a harmless form of a pathogen so it builds memory. Types include live-attenuated, inactivated, subunit and mRNA vaccines.
layers.deeper: Smallpox was eradicated in 1980 through vaccination. When enough people are immune (herd immunity threshold ≈ 1 − 1/R₀), outbreaks fade.
layers.expert: Adjuvants boost responses; mRNA-LNP vaccines encode antigens and were deployed in 2020–21 (Nobel 2023 for nucleoside modification). Vaccine effectiveness is evaluated by randomised trials and observational data; waning immunity and escape require boosters.

layers.basics: Allergies are overreactions to harmless substances, driven by IgE. In autoimmune disease the body attacks its own tissues, as in type 1 diabetes and rheumatoid arthritis.
layers.deeper: Gell–Coombs types I–IV classify hypersensitivity. Anaphylaxis can be life threatening and is treated with adrenaline.
layers.expert: Autoimmune diseases affect ≈ 5–8% of people, mostly women. Triggers combine genes (HLA), infection and environment; molecular mimicry is one proposed mechanism.

layers.basics: Immunodeficiency can be inherited or acquired (HIV). Transplants are rejected unless donors are matched and immune responses are suppressed.
layers.deeper: Tolerance means not attacking self. Immunosuppressive drugs like cyclosporine prevent rejection but raise infection risk.
layers.expert: SCID ("bubble boy") was the first target for gene therapy. Graft-versus-host disease occurs when donor T cells attack the recipient. Pregnancy involves unique fetal tolerance mechanisms.

layers.basics: Immunotherapy removes brakes on T cells (checkpoint inhibitors) or engineers T cells to attack tumours (CAR-T).
layers.deeper: Allison and Honjo won the 2018 Nobel for checkpoint blockade. Responses can be durable in some melanoma and lung cancer patients.
layers.expert: Response rates vary (≈ 20–40% in many tumours); biomarkers include PD-L1 and tumour mutational burden. Side effects include immune-related adverse events.

layers.basics: ELISA uses an enzyme-linked antibody to produce a colour change that tells how much antigen is present.
layers.deeper: Lateral-flow tests (pregnancy, rapid antigen) use antibodies on a strip. Flow cytometry counts and sorts cells by fluorescent antibody labels.
layers.expert: Sandwich ELISA sensitivities reach ≈ pg/mL. Monoclonal antibodies (Köhler and Milstein, 1975) provide specificity. Controls and standard curves are essential for quantitation.
